text: The Moon's average distance from Earth is about 384,400 kilometres.
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

text: The Moon is about 3,500 kilometres in diameter (3,474.8 km).
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

text: Scenario assumption: the second Moon orbits at about 700,000 kilometres, nearly twice the Moon's distance (700,000 / 384,400 is about 1.8).
source: Scenario choice by the script; ratio computed from NASA Moon Fact Sheet distance

text: The Moon has about one eighty-first of Earth's mass.
as_written: about one eighty-first of the mass of Earth
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (mass ratio 0.0123)

text: Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth.
source: Distance 384,400 km divided by speed of light 299,792 km/s (NIST/SI definition; NASA Moon Fact Sheet)

text: Light from a body at 700,000 km takes about 2.3 seconds to arrive.
source: 700,000 km divided by speed of light 299,792 km/s (SI defined value)

text: The full Moon is roughly 400,000 times dimmer than the Sun (apparent magnitudes about -12.7 versus -26.7).
as_written: roughly 400,000 times dimmer than the Sun
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet and Sun Fact Sheet apparent magnitudes

text: At 700,000 km the second Moon's apparent area, and so its light, is about a quarter of the Moon's (inverse-square on angular size).
as_written: about a quarter of the first
source: Geometry using NASA Moon Fact Sheet distance and diameter

text: The Moon spans about half a degree of sky.
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (mean angular diameter about 0.52 degrees)

text: A 3,475 km body at 700,000 km spans about 0.28 degrees.
source: Geometry from NASA Moon Fact Sheet diameter

text: The Moon moves against the stars by about 13 degrees per day (360 degrees over 27.3 days).
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet sidereal period 27.32 days

text: A body orbiting at 700,000 km moves about 5 degrees per day (360 degrees over about 67 days).
source: Kepler's third law applied to NASA Moon Fact Sheet orbit values

text: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look about the same size.
as_written: about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away
source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet and Moon Fact Sheet; NASA eclipse explanations

text: The Sun's apparent diameter is about half a degree, larger than 0.28 degrees, so the second Moon could not cause total eclipses.
as_written: The Sun and Moon both span about half a degree
source: NASA Sun Fact Sheet (about 0.53 degrees)

text: The lunar tidal cycle is about 12 hours and 25 minutes.
source: NOAA Tides and Currents (tidal day 24h50m, semidiurnal period)

text: Tidal force falls as the cube of distance.
as_written: falls off with the cube of distance
source: NOAA / standard tidal theory

text: Doubling distance cuts tidal force by a factor of eight.
source: Inverse-cube law, standard tidal theory

text: At 700,000 km the second Moon's tide is about 17 percent of the Moon's ((384,400/700,000)^3 = 0.166).
source: Inverse-cube tidal scaling with NASA Moon Fact Sheet distance

text: The Sun's tide is a little under half the Moon's, about 46 percent.
as_written: a little under half as strong
source: NOAA Tides and Currents (Sun's tidal force about 46% of Moon's)

text: The Sun adds roughly 46 percent to the lunar tide at spring tide.
source: NOAA Tides and Currents

text: Biggest tides would be about 11 to 12 percent higher (1.63 versus 1.46).
source: Computed from NOAA tidal ratios and inverse-cube scaling

text: Open-ocean tides are less than a metre.
source: NOAA National Ocean Service tides education

text: The Bay of Fundy tidal range exceeds 15 metres (16.3 m at Burntcoat Head).
source: Canadian Hydrographic Service / Parks Canada

text: An 11 percent increase on about 16 metres is nearly two extra metres.
source: Computed from Canadian Hydrographic Service range and the tidal ratios above

text: Great Barrier Reef corals mass spawn a few nights after a full Moon in late spring.
as_written: a few nights after a full Moon in late spring
source: Harrison et al. 1984, Science; Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

text: The Moon's sidereal orbital period is 27.3 days.
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: The synodic month (phase cycle) is 29.5 days.
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: By Kepler's third law an orbit at 700,000 km takes about 67 days.
source: Kepler's third law applied to NASA Moon Fact Sheet orbit values

text: Two moons with 27.3 and 67 day periods align about every 46 days.
source: Synodic period computed from Kepler's third law

text: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
source: NASA / US Naval Observatory moonrise data

text: A body with a 67-day period would rise about 22 minutes later each day.
source: Computed from Kepler's third law and Earth's rotation rate

text: The Moon recedes at about 3.8 centimetres per year.
source: Apollo Lunar Laser Ranging experiments; NASA

text: Earth's day lengthens by about 1.7 milliseconds per century due to tidal friction.
source: Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016, Proc. Royal Society A; IERS

text: Devonian fossil corals show about 400 days per year around 400 million years ago.
source: Wells 1963, Nature; Scrutton 1964

text: Devonian period was about 400 million years ago.
source: International Commission on Stratigraphy

text: Days then were about 22 hours long.
source: Wells 1963 (400 days per year implies about 22 hours); Williams 2000, Reviews of Geophysics

text: Tidal braking torque scales with the inverse sixth power of distance.
source: Standard tidal friction theory, e.g. Murray and Dermott, Solar System Dynamics

text: At 1.8 times the distance the torque is about 3 percent of the Moon's ((384,400/700,000)^6 = 0.027).
source: Computed from sixth-power scaling and NASA Moon Fact Sheet distance

text: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4 degrees.
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: The tilt varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over about 41,000 years.
as_written: between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years
source: Milankovitch cycle values, NASA Earth Observatory

text: Laskar 1993 found that without the Moon Earth's tilt could wander chaotically from near zero to about 85 degrees.
as_written: anywhere from nearly zero to about 85 degrees
source: Laskar, Joutel and Robutel 1993, Nature, 'Stabilization of the Earth's obliquity by the Moon'

text: Laskar published this in 1993.
source: Laskar, Joutel and Robutel 1993, Nature

text: A 2012 study by Lissauer and colleagues found tilt variations without the Moon are much milder.
as_written: a 2012 study by Jack Lissauer and colleagues
source: Lissauer, Barnes and Chambers 2012, Icarus, 'Obliquity variations of a moonless Earth'

text: Earth's Hill sphere reaches about 1.5 million kilometres.
source: NASA / standard Hill sphere calculation (Earth Fact Sheet values)

text: Prograde orbits are stable out to about half the Hill radius, roughly 730,000 km.
source: Domingos, Winter and Yokoyama 2006, Astronomy and Astrophysics (0.4895 Hill radii)

text: Gladman 1993 gave a stability criterion of about three and a half mutual Hill radii of separation (2 root 3).
as_written: about three and a half of their mutual Hill radii
source: Gladman 1993, Icarus, 'Dynamics of systems of two close planets'

text: Gladman's criterion was published in 1993.
source: Gladman 1993, Icarus

text: Applying the criterion to two Moon-mass bodies puts the outer one at about 800,000 km or more.
source: Computed from Gladman 1993 criterion with NASA Moon and Earth masses and distance

text: L4 and L5 sit 60 degrees ahead of and behind the Moon.
as_written: 60 degrees ahead of and behind the Moon
source: Standard Lagrange point geometry; NASA

text: Stability at L4 and L5 requires the primary to be at least about 25 times the secondary's mass (24.96).
as_written: at least about 25 times the mass
source: Routh stability criterion, Murray and Dermott, Solar System Dynamics

text: Earth is about 81 times the mass of the Moon.
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: Kordylewski reported dust cloud candidates at the Earth-Moon Lagrange points in 1961.
source: Kordylewski 1961, Acta Astronomica / Astronomical Society publications

text: A Hungarian team reported polarised light from dust clouds at those points in 2018; this is still debated.
source: Slíz-Balogh, Barta and Horváth 2018, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

text: Jutzi and Asphaug proposed in 2011 that a companion moon formed the far side highlands.
as_written: In 2011, Martin Jutzi and Erik Asphaug
source: Jutzi and Asphaug 2011, Nature, 'Forming the lunar farside highlands by accretion of a companion moon'

text: The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago.
source: NASA Lunar and Planetary Institute; Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances

text: The proposed impact speed was about 2.5 kilometres per second.
as_written: about two and a half kilometres per second
source: Jutzi and Asphaug 2011, Nature
